title: Kanthaka's heart
hook: a later telling: the horse, sent home without him, dies of grief

segments.voice: Yesterday, pabbajja: the going forth, the hair cut with a sword on the riverbank. Your line was less to carry. What small vanity did you set down? Day forty.

If you've ever had a dog, you know the look. You pick up your keys, and before you've even reached the door, the dog knows. The ears drop. The eyes follow you. And when you come home, the joy at the door is so big it seems like it might break something. Animals love us in a way that doesn't ask questions. On the riverbank, the prince, now in his plain robe, turns to Channa and tells him to go home. Take the jewels. Take Kanthaka. Tell my father I'm well. Channa begs to stay. The prince says no. And the white horse, standing there, hears it all. Today, Kanthaka's heart.
screen: `THE DOG KNOWS YOU'RE LEAVING.` → `GO HOME, CHANNA.` → `THE HORSE HEARS IT ALL.`

segments.voice: This part comes from the later tellings, not the oldest suttas, and it's one of the most loved. In one version, Kanthaka kneels and licks his master's feet, weeping. In the Pali telling, Kanthaka understands he will never see his master again. He walks away with Channa, and as the prince passes out of sight, the horse's heart breaks, and he dies right there on the road. Channa goes home alone, with two griefs to carry. And then the story does something tender. It says Kanthaka was reborn among the gods, in a heavenly realm, as a being named Kanthaka, because of his love and his service. The horse's grief wasn't wasted. Why would Buddhists keep a story like this? Because in the Buddhist view, animals aren't scenery. They're sentient beings, beings who feel, who can suffer, who can love. The first precept, to refrain from killing, reaches to them. The Buddha's famous teaching on loving-kindness wishes happiness to all beings, the weak and the strong, the seen and the unseen. And in the Jataka stories of his past lives, the Buddha-to-be is again and again an animal: a monkey, a deer, a hare, an elephant. Kanthaka's heart says the same thing in one image. Love is not a human privilege. When we leave, they grieve too. Whether or not you take the heavenly rebirth literally, the story asks you to take the grief seriously.
screen: `A LATER TELLING.` · `THE HORSE'S HEART BREAKS.` · `ANIMALS ARE BEINGS WHO FEEL.` · `A MONKEY, A DEER, A HARE.` · then, large: `THEY GRIEVE TOO.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let the breath slow. Bring to mind an animal who loved you, or who you loved. A pet from childhood, one you have now, a neighbor's dog who always came to the fence, a bird that visits the window. Picture it clearly. The weight of it leaning on you, the sound it made when you came home. Let yourself feel the love that animal gave without asking for anything. If you'd like, silently wish it well: may you be happy, may you be free from fear. The bell holds the time.
Kanthaka's heart. The white horse who, in the later telling, died of grief when his master sent him home, and was reborn among the gods.
Your line: they grieve too. Today, be gentle with one animal, a pet, a bird, even an insect you'd usually swat, and remember it feels. Day forty.

howItsDone: Buddhists extend the first precept, not killing, to animals, and many practice loving-kindness toward all beings; in some countries, people release captive animals or birds as an act of merit.

fork.setup: you're the prince, now robed. Channa begs to stay with you. what do you do?
options: let Channa and Kanthaka come along.

keep the horse, send Channa home.
fork.reveal: he sends them home. the horse hears it, and in the telling, his heart breaks on the road.

original.note: Pali: the prince's white horse, reborn in the telling as a heavenly being of the same name.

trapdoor: what you thought: a sad story about a horse.
what it means: animals feel, love and grieve. the story asks you to take their grief seriously.
what a scholar hears: the Nidanakatha has Kanthaka die of a broken heart and be reborn in the Tavatimsa heaven as the god Kanthaka; the Buddhacarita has him weep and lick the prince's feet.

notes: Kanthaka licking the prince's feet and weeping: Buddhacarita canto 6. Confirm canto.
Kanthaka reborn in Tavatimsa as a god named Kanthaka: Nidanakatha (also the Vimanavatthu has a Kanthaka story). Confirm.
Metta Sutta paraphrased (weak or strong, seen or unseen); confirm.
